Data verification is very effective in ensuring the data entered is correct.
Double entry can be used, where a user keys in data twice, and the system will automatically check if the two inputs match, if not, the user will be alerted there has been an error during data entry, and to amend the data input.
Proof reading can also be used, where the user keys in the data, and then compares it to the original source, ensuring they both match.
Together, these two methods of data verification will stop most data entry errors, including transposition errors, however, if there are several numbers wrong, it is not guaranteed to always work.
note: Quality of written communication assessed. Examiner's comment: "Only 1 statement about proof reading". The question says DISCUSS the effectiveness: it needs the limitations too (e.g. verification can't catch data that was wrong on the source document; both methods take extra time).

Cache memory: Cache memory stores the most frequently accessed ✓ data/instructions closer to the CPU, in a faster media allowing this data to be accessed quicker. The cache memory is always searched ✓ first before the main memory.

A hash total is a type of batch total used for error checking, which does not have a meaningful ✓ use other than error checking, for example, the total number of staff that worked that week is 4 ✓.

A multitasking operating system allows a single user to run several applications at a time, when they are only ever actually running one at any given time. The processor does this by quickly switching between applications, sharing/allocating processing resources, e.g. memory to each application, making it appear to the user that several applications are running at the same time.
This could be used by a computer system, where an employee has a spreadsheet of sales data open, at the same time as a word processor, allowing them to create a write up on sales, without having to close an app to see the other every time.
A multiprocessing operating system makes use of two or more processors/cores, where two copies of the same application can be executed at the same time, and each core could be working on a different part of the task. The cores could also be working together on the same task.
In an organisation this could be used if there is a powerful server at the centre of the network, which can accommodate several users at a time, giving each of their tasks some of the processors/cores from the powerful server PC.
note: Quality of written communication assessed. A clear, well-organised answer that defines both and gives an example of each in use, so it reaches the top band.
